titleEn: Laws of Hammurabi — §215–240: surgeons, builders and boatmen (xxxiv 55 – xxxvi 80)
part: Laws §215–240 · surgeons, builders & boatmen (Col. xxxiv 55 – xxxvi 80)
about: Twenty-six laws on the people whose work can go wrong. The surgeon comes first (§215–223): a physician who opens a wound or the nagabtu (a word I cannot read, perhaps near the eye) and heals the man takes ten shekels from a man, five from a commoner, two from the owner of a slave (§215–217); if the patient dies, or loses his eye, the surgeon’s hands are cut off (§218), and for a commoner’s slave who dies he replaces the slave (§219). The animal doctor’s fees follow (§224–225), then the barber who shaves a slave’s mark off a slave that is not his: his hands are cut off, and the man who (as I read an unread verb) tricked him is killed and hanged at his gate (§226–227). The builder is next (§228–233): fee by the area built; and if the house falls and kills its owner the builder is killed, if it kills the owner’s son the builder’s son is killed, if a slave a slave, if goods the goods are replaced and the house rebuilt at his own cost. The last laws are the boatmen’s (§234–240): their fee for work on a boat (caulking, I think), their liability when a boat is sunk or its cargo lost, a boatman’s yearly hire, and a collision. Several words of the boat laws I cannot read and say so. Harper’s line numerals in col. xxxiv run one ahead of his own §-headings up to §221; I follow the running numerals. §239–240 are partly broken, and Harper’s square brackets are kept.

sentences.l: If a-physician a-man a-wound heavy with-the-GÍR.NI of-bronze has-made-and,
sentences.i: If a physician has made a severe wound in a man with a bronze knife,
sentences.n: Surgeons’ fees and penalties open here (§215–223: men and slaves; §224–225: animals; §226–227: the barber; §228–233: builders; §234–240: boatmen). Harper’s line numerals in col. xxxiv run one ahead of his own §-headings through §221; I follow the running numerals (they agree with the plate’s margin numbers 55, 60, 65 …). The usual šumma pattern: šumma asûm awīlam ṣimmam kabtam … īpušma, “if a physician has made a severe wound in a man …”. A.ZU is the two signs A and ZU with no ending; the case (asûm here) is the grammar’s. GÍR.NI is two signs I leave unread: some cutting tool (a knife); the exact kind I cannot say. siparrim “of bronze” is three signs, UD.KA.BAR, with no ending written (Harper’s list no. 148). ṣimmam: ZI read ṣi (Harper prints zi); “wound” is Harper’s sense, not derivable from the grammar (UNCERTAIN). kabtam “heavy, severe”. īpušma: i-bu-uš-ma, the sign BU read pu; preterite of epēšum “to do, make”, with -ma joining the next clause.

sentences.i: and has healed the man,
sentences.n: ubtalliṭ is the perfect (infixed -ta-) of the D-stem of balāṭum “to live”; the D-stem makes “live” into “make live”, i.e. “heal”. The subject is still the physician, and the verb finishes the first condition of §215 (he made the wound, and he healed the man).

sentences.l: or the-nagabtu of-a-man with-the-GÍR.NI of-bronze he-has-opened-and,
sentences.i: or has opened a man’s nagabtu (something of or near the eye, uncertain) with a bronze knife,
sentences.n: ù lū “or”: ù is the conjunction (the sign U3, not the verb prefix u-), lū “either, or”. nagabti is Harper’s na-gab-ti; I cannot read the word: the context (the next line heals “the man’s eye”) suggests a part of or near the eye, and the knife opens it; UNCERTAIN. iptēma is the preterite of petûm “to open” with -ma (“and”): “he opened and …”.

sentences.i: and has healed the man’s eye,
sentences.n: īn awīlim “the eye of a man”: īn (i-in) is the bound form of īnum “eye” before the genitive awīlim. Harper’s line 64 again has ubtalliṭ, “has healed”. The two conditions of §215 (a wound healed; the nagabtu opened and the eye healed) share one fee.

sentences.i: he shall take ten shekels of silver.
sentences.n: The fee. ešret “ten” is the single corner wedge; šiqil “shekel” is the sign GÍN; kaspim “silver” is KÙ.BABBAR, two signs and nothing after them (no -im is written on the plate; the genitive is the grammar’s). ileqqi, i-li-qi (the sign KI read qi₂), is the present of leqûm “to take”: “he shall take”. Present tense is the code’s tense for the penalty. The three fees run in the order of rank: a man (awīlum) 10 shekels, a commoner (muškēnum) 5, a man’s slave 2 (§215–217).

sentences.i: If it is a commoner’s son,
sentences.n: mār muškēnim “son of a commoner”: DUMU, then MAŠ.EN.KAK (three signs, no ending), the genitive being the grammar’s. A muškēnum is a free man of the lower class, neither a full awīlum nor a slave. The subject is still the patient: the same operation, with the fee scaled down.

sentences.i: he shall take five shekels of silver.
sentences.n: ḫamšat “five” is the sign IA5 (five wedges in two groups); the rest as in §215.

sentences.i: If it is a man’s slave,
sentences.n: warad awīlim “slave of a man”: ARAD with no ending (the sign is Harper’s no. 16), then awīlim.

sentences.l: the-owner of-the-slave to-the-physician two shekel of-silver he-shall-give.
sentences.i: the slave’s owner shall give the physician two shekels of silver.
sentences.n: Here the owner pays, because the slave cannot. bēl wardim “the owner of the slave”: be-el (the signs BE, EL), ARAD bare. ana asîm “to the physician”: A.ZU, the case again from the grammar. inaddin (i-na-ad-di-in) is the present of nadānum “to give”. šinā “two” is the two upright wedges.

sentences.l: If a-physician a-man a-wound heavy with-the-GÍR.NI of-bronze has-made-and,
sentences.i: If a physician has made a severe wound in a man with a bronze knife,
sentences.n: Same opening as §215, now with the bad outcome. Harper prints zi-im-ma-am for ṣimmam here; the sign is ZI, read ṣi as before.

sentences.i: and has caused the man to die,
sentences.n: uštamīt, uš-ta-mi-it, is the perfect of the Š-stem of mâtum “to die”; the Š-stem is the causative: “has made (him) die”, “has killed”. The plain statement of the code: the death is the physician’s doing, and the penalty follows in the last unit.

sentences.l: or the-nagabtu of-a-man with-the-GÍR.NI of-bronze he-has-opened-and the-eye of-a-man he-has-destroyed,
sentences.i: or has opened a man’s nagabtu (uncertain) with a bronze knife and has destroyed the man’s eye,
sentences.n: As §215, with the opposite end: uḫtabbit is the perfect of the D-stem of ḫabātum, rendered “has destroyed” as in the talion laws (§196–200), where the grammar cannot say more than that (UNCERTAIN as a word; the sense is the law’s).

sentences.i: they shall cut off his hands.
sentences.n: The penalty is the surgeon’s hands, not a fine. rittēšu “his hands”: the signs UM and ME (the vertical-and-bar sign) and ŠU, as in §195, where the identification of the second sign and the plural (hands or hand) are UNCERTAIN; Harper writes rittê-šu. inakkisū “they shall cut off”: i-na-ki-su here, three plain syllables (§195 has an extra ak); present, plural, of nakāsum, an impersonal “they” (the code does not say who does it).

sentences.l: If a-physician a-wound heavy a-slave of-a-commoner
sentences.i: If a physician has made a severe wound on a commoner’s slave
sentences.n: The sentence runs through two units: the wound and the victim here, the knife and the verbs next. warad muškēnim “slave of a commoner”: ARAD and MAŠ.EN.KAK, both bare. Harper prints zi-ma-am with a single m (his zi-im-ma-am elsewhere); I keep his spelling (ṣi-ma-am) and read the same word, ṣimmam.

sentences.i: with a bronze knife, and has killed him,
sentences.n: The verbs of the protasis, as in §218: īpušma, uštamīt.

sentences.i: he shall replace the slave with a slave.
sentences.n: The penalty is like for like. wardam kīma wardim: ARAD twice, bare; the accusative wardam (what he gives back) and the genitive after kīma are the grammar’s. iriab, i-ri-ab (three signs here; i-ri-a-ab later in the part), is the present of riābum “to replace, make good”, the house verb for restitution.

sentences.l: If his-nagabtu with-the-GÍR.NI of-bronze he-has-opened-and his-eye he-has-destroyed,
sentences.i: If he has opened his nagabtu (uncertain) with a bronze knife and destroyed his eye,
sentences.n: “His” is the slave of §219. nagabtašu, na-gab-ta-šu: the word of §215, with -šu “his”; UNCERTAIN as there. Harper’s uḫ-tab-da(=it) is a carver’s slip that he corrects in his own parentheses: the last sign is da, where bi-it (uḫtabbit, as in §218) is meant; I write the sign as it stands and say uḫtabbit.

sentences.i: he shall pay silver, half his price.
sentences.n: For a commoner’s slave the penalty is money: half the slave’s price. kaspam is KÙ.BABBAR, bare; mišil “half”, three syllables (mi-ši-il); šīmišu “his price” is the sign ŠÁM (Harper’s no. 83) and ŠU, with -šu the slave’s; išaqqal (i-ša-qal) “he shall weigh out, pay”. Harper’s i-ṣ̌a-qal in his note is a printing blemish; the plate shows the ordinary I ŠA GAL.

sentences.l: If a-physician the-bone of-a-man the-break has-made-whole,
sentences.i: If a physician has made whole a man’s broken bone,
sentences.n: eṣemti awīlim “the bone of a man” is NER.PAD.DU (three signs, no ending) and awīlim. šebirtam “a break, fracture” is Harper’s še-bi-ir-tam (from šebērum “to break”); uštalim, uš-ta-li-im, is the perfect of the Š-stem of šalāmum “to be whole, sound”: “has made whole”.

sentences.i: or has healed a sick sinew (?),
sentences.n: Harper prints še-ir ḫa-nam as two words; the spelling še-ir-ḫa-nam reads šer’ānam, a word for a body part (the ʾ is written with the sign ḪA). “Sinew, muscle” is a guess from the sound and the sense (something that can be sick and healed); UNCERTAIN. marṣam “sick”, ubtalliṭ as in §215.

sentences.l: the-owner of-the-wound to-the-physician five shekel of-silver he-shall-give.
sentences.i: the patient (lit. the owner of the wound) shall give the physician five shekels of silver.
sentences.n: bēl ṣimmim “the owner of the wound” is the patient; ṣimmim is Harper’s ṣi-im-mi-im (the genitive of ṣimmum, uncertain as in §215).

sentences.i: If it is a commoner’s son,
sentences.n: As §216: the same operation on a commoner’s son.

sentences.i: he shall give three shekels of silver.
sentences.n: šalāš “three” is the three wedges (THREE). The fee for a broken bone or a sick sinew is lower for a commoner (3) than for a man (5).

sentences.i: If it is a man’s slave,

sentences.l: the-owner of-the-slave to-the-physician two shekel of-silver he-shall-give.
sentences.i: the slave’s owner shall give the physician two shekels of silver.
If a physician of an ox or an ass (a physician who treats animals),
sentences.n: From here the patient is an animal. A.ZU alpim u lū imērim “a physician of an ox or an ass”: alpim is GU₄ (the single sign of Harper’s no. 109) and imērim is ANŠE (his no. 91), both with no ending written; ù lū is “or”. The words describe the physician; the wound and the cure follow.

sentences.l: either an-ox or an-ass a-wound heavy he-has-made-and he-has-healed,
sentences.i: if he has made a severe wound on an ox or an ass and has healed it,
sentences.n: lū … u lū “either … or”. alpam, imēram are accusatives (the objects), written GU₄ and ANŠE bare. ṣimmam kabtam īpušma ubtalliṭ is §215’s clause again; the object of ubtalliṭ is the animal, not written.

sentences.l: the-owner of-the-ox or of-the-ass one-sixth of-silver
sentences.i: the owner of the ox or the ass (shall give) one sixth (of a shekel) of silver
sentences.n: šuššat is IGI.VI.GAL: IGI, the six wedges (three over three) and GAL, the way a fraction “one sixth” is written, here before kaspim. The unit is not written; “shekel” is the natural unit (as in the other fees). šuššat is reconstructed from the pattern, as for the thirds.

sentences.i: to the physician as his fee.
sentences.n: idīšu “his hire, fee” (the case vowel is the grammar’s; an accusative would be idāšu, so the vowel is UNCERTAIN): Harper’s ID-šu; the sign is the A₂ sign (Á, the sign that elsewhere writes id), with ŠU. The line carries the verb of the previous unit: “the owner … shall give, to the physician, as his fee, one sixth …”.

sentences.l: If an-ox or an-ass a-wound heavy he-has-made-and he-has-caused-to-die,
sentences.i: If he has made a severe wound on an ox or an ass and has killed it,
sentences.n: The same physician, the same wound, the opposite result. ZI is read ṣi in ṣimmam (Harper prints zi); a raised b in Harper’s col. xxxv marks only a second tier on the same stele line.

sentences.l: one-fourth his-price to-the-owner of-the-ox or of-the-ass he-shall-give.
sentences.i: he shall give one quarter of its price to the owner of the ox or the ass.
sentences.n: IGI.IV.GAL is the fraction “one quarter”: IGI, the four wedges (two over two), GAL; rebūt is reconstructed from the pattern (UNCERTAIN as a spoken form). šīmišu “his (its) price”, ŠÁM-šu as in §220; the last verb is written i-na-ad-di-in with the acute on di in Harper (a print mark; the plate has the ordinary DI).

sentences.l: If a-barber without the-owner of-the-slave the-slave-mark
sentences.i: If a barber, without the slave’s owner, (has shaved off) the slave-mark
sentences.n: gallābum “barber” is ŠU.I (two signs, bare; Harper’s no. 138). balum is “without” (ba-lum). abbutti is Harper’s ab-bu-ti: abbuttum, as in §146 (“puts the slave-mark (?) on her”); the sense “slave-mark” is the later dictionaries’, not Harper’s (he has “service, slavery”), and that it was a hair-style is not in the text at all: UNCERTAIN. The form is the construct, “the abbuttum of …” (before wardi). The verb is on the next unit.

sentences.i: of a slave who is not his, has shaved it off,
sentences.n: wardi lā šēm “of a slave not his”: ARAD bare; Harper’s la še-e-im (three signs ŠE E IM) reads šēm, a form of the pronoun, UNCERTAIN: the sense (a slave who does not belong to him) is the context’s. ugallib is the D-stem of galābum “to shave” (infinitive gullubum) (the barber’s own verb, gallābum): “he has shaved off”.

sentences.i: they shall cut off that barber’s hands.
sentences.n: rittē is UM.ME again (two signs, bare); gallābim šuāti “of that barber”: ŠU.I, then šu-a-ti “that” (šuāti). inakkisū is written i-na-ak-ki-su here.

sentences.i: If a man has deceived (?) the barber and
sentences.n: idāṣma, i-da-aṣ-ma (the AZ sign read aṣ): I cannot read the verb. The sense “deceived” is not derivable from the form (the lemma is only the form, idāṣ); it is the sense the law seems to need: the barber shaves the slave-mark without knowing it is not his to shave (below, §227 ends with the barber’s oath that he did not do it knowingly); UNCERTAIN.

sentences.i: and he (the barber) has shaved off the slave-mark of a slave not his,
sentences.n: ugdallib, ug-da-al-li-ib, is the D perfect of galābum (§226 has ugallib).

sentences.i: they shall kill that man and
sentences.n: The deceiver’s punishment, plain and severe: death, and hanging at his own gate. idukkūšuma: i-du-uk-ku-šu-ma, the verb idukkū “they shall kill” (present plural of dâkum, an impersonal “they”), with -šu “him” and -ma “and”; the third sign is UG (box and triangle), as in §210.

sentences.i: and hang him at his gate.
sentences.n: bābīšu “his gate”: KÁ (the gate sign, Harper’s no. 64) and ŠU. iḫallalūšu: i-ḫa-al-la-lu-šu, present plural of ḫalālum with -šu “him”; “hang” is the usual sense of this verb, not something the form shows (UNCERTAIN) (Harper prints the word over two tiers of the same line).

sentences.l: the-barber in knowing not I-have-shaved he-shall-swear-and he-shall-be-released.
sentences.i: The barber shall swear, ‘I did not shave him knowingly’, and shall be released.
sentences.n: The barber’s defence is an oath. ina idû lā ugallibu “knowingly I did not shave”: idû (i-du-u) is the infinitive of edûm “to know” after ina, “in knowing”; ugallibu is first person with the subjunctive -u (in a quotation). itammama (i-tam-ma-ma): present of tamûm “to swear”, with -ma; ūtaššar is the Dt of wašārum, “he shall be released”, as in earlier parts.

sentences.l: If a-builder a-house for-a-man has-made-and has-completed-for-him,
sentences.i: If a builder has built a house for a man and has completed it for him,
sentences.n: bānûm “builder” is the sign Harper numbers 168 (one sign: a bar-and-vertical frame with a small diamond low in it; the same sign stands alone at XXXV 64, 72, 75, 93 and 98); I key it ŠITIM (Unicode ŠITA, tentative). On this line šum is drawn in two parts, an arrowhead and a hatched triangle, and ma is the bar-and-vertical sign, so the line is šum, ma, ŠITIM with no further sign before the builder’s. bītam “house” is É, bare. īpušma “he built (made)”; ušaklilšum, u-ša-ak-li-il-šum, is the Š of kalālum “to be complete” with -šum “for him”: “has completed it for him”.

sentences.l: for 1 SAR of-house two shekel of-silver as-his-gift he-shall-give-him.
sentences.i: he shall give him two shekels of silver as his gift for each SAR of house.
sentences.n: SAR is a unit of area (the plot a house stands on), left unread. ana 1 SAR bītim “for one SAR of house”; qīštišu, qi-iš-ti-šu (Harper’s qi-iš-ti-šu, the sign KI read qi₂), is qīštum “gift”, -šu “his”: the builder’s fee is called his gift; inaddiššum “he shall give him”.

sentences.i: If a builder has built a house for a man
sentences.n: The builder’s death penalties: the two clauses that follow are the code’s plain rule that a builder pays with his life when his work kills. Same words as §228.

sentences.i: and has not made his work strong,
sentences.n: šipiršu “his work” (ši-bi-ir-šu: the sign BI for pi); udanninma is the D of danānum “to be strong”, “make strong”, with -ma: lā udanninma “and has not made … strong”.

sentences.l: the-house which-he-built has-fallen-and the-owner of-the-house he-has-caused-to-die,
sentences.i: and the house that he built has fallen and has caused the owner of the house to die,
sentences.n: bītum īpušu “the house that he built”: īpušu is īpuš plus the subjunctive -u (a relative clause with no ša). imqutma: im-ku-ut-ma, preterite (imqut) of maqātum “to fall” with -ma. bēl bītim “the owner of the house”.

sentences.i: that builder shall be killed.
sentences.n: The penalty: iddâk, id-da-ak, is the N-stem (passive) of dâkum “to kill”: “he shall be killed”. šū “that (one)”. The N-stem passive is the code’s house form for an execution; the active idukkū “they shall kill” is used when the victim is a third person (§230).

sentences.i: If it has caused the death of the owner’s son,
sentences.n: mār bēl bītim “the son of the owner of the house”: DUMU, then bēl bītim (BE EL, É). The subject is the fallen house; the verb is uštamīt again.

sentences.i: they shall kill the son of that builder.
sentences.n: A life for a life, in the next generation: mār bānîm šuāti. Harper’s mark on the second i of bânîm is ambiguous between a circumflex and an acute; the sign is the same bānû sign. idukkū (i-du-uk-ku) is active, plural: “they shall kill”.

sentences.i: If it has caused the death of a slave of the owner of the house,
sentences.n: warad bēl bītim “a slave of the owner of the house”: ARAD, then bēl bītim.

sentences.l: a-slave like a-slave to-the-owner of-the-house he-shall-give.
sentences.i: he shall give the owner of the house a slave for a slave.
sentences.n: As §219: wardam kīma wardim; inaddin “he shall give”.

sentences.i: If he has destroyed property,
sentences.n: ŠA.GA is makkūrum “property” (as in earlier parts: Harper’s ŠA.GA; the signs are keyed GAR and GA there). On the plate (XXXV 82, 90; XXXVI 22) the first sign is drawn like the ŠÀ sign of Harper’s bušu entry (no. 209: a box with a vertical and a diagonal) and the second like his no. 128 (horizontal wedges and an arrowhead); the key GAR (𒃻) for the first sign follows the eight earlier parts for consistency, not the plate, and the identification is UNCERTAIN (modern editions read NÍG.GA). In this line šum is drawn in two parts, an arrowhead and a hatched triangle, and ma is the bar-and-vertical sign; nothing stands between ma and the first sign of ŠA.GA. uḫtalliq: perfect of the D-stem of ḫalāqum “to be lost”, “make lost, destroy”.

sentences.i: he shall replace whatever he has destroyed,
sentences.n: mimma ša uḫalliqu “whatever he destroyed”: the relative ša, then the verb with the subjunctive -u (u-ḫal-li-qu₂, KU read qu₂). iriab, i-ri-ab, “he shall replace”.

sentences.l: and because the-house he-built not he-made-strong-and it-fell,
sentences.i: and, because he did not make the house that he built strong, and it fell,
sentences.n: ù aššum “and because”. bītam īpušu: the house that he built (subjunctive -u). lā udanninuma: the subjunctive -u before -ma, not a plural (the same builder). imqutu: imqut with the subjunctive -u. Harper prints bitam without a circumflex here; the sign is É as elsewhere.

sentences.l: from the-property of-himself the-house which-fell he-shall-rebuild.
sentences.i: he shall rebuild the house that fell out of his own property.
sentences.n: ina makkūr ramānišu “from his own property”: ramānišu (ra-ma-ni-šu) “himself” with -šu. ippeš, i-ib-bi-eš, is the present of epēšum “to make”, written with ibbi for ippi: “he shall rebuild”.

sentences.i: If a builder has built a house for a man
sentences.n: No death here: only the wall. Same opening as §229.

sentences.i: and has not made his work right (?), and a wall has given way (?),
sentences.n: Two verbs I cannot read. uštēṣbima, uš-te-iṣ-bi-ma, is a Š perfect of a root I do not know; “make right, true” is a guess from the context (the work was not done as it should have been); UNCERTAIN. iqtup, iq-tu-up, has the shape of a preterite of qatāpum (a perfect would be iqtatap); “has given way” (of a wall) is likewise only the context’s sense; UNCERTAIN. igārum “wall” is É.GAR₈ (É and a sign Harper shows after É in his list no. 121 igaru; I key it GAR₃, the nearest sign in the glossary).

sentences.l: that builder with-the-silver of-himself that wall he-shall-make-strong.
sentences.i: that builder shall strengthen that wall at his own expense (with his own silver).
sentences.n: ina kaspim ramānišu “with silver of himself”: the builder pays from his own pocket. igaram šuāti is “that wall”: É.GAR₈ (Harper normalizes igaram; no ending is written). udannan, u-dan-na-an, present of the D of danānum: “he shall make strong”.

sentences.l: If a-boatman a-boat of-60 kor for-a-man he-has-ipḫi,
sentences.i: If a boatman has caulked (?) a boat of sixty kor for a man,
sentences.n: From here the boatmen. malaḫum “boatman, sailor” is MÁ.LAḪ₄: MÁ and two DU signs (LAḪ₄ is DU.DU; Harper’s no. 58 shows the same three pieces). elippi “boat of” is GIŠ.MÁ (two signs, bare; Harper’s no. 108 elippu). 60 kor is the 60 wedge and GUR; kur is the large grain-measure. ipḫi, ip-ḫi: a verb I cannot read; “caulk” (make watertight) is not derivable from the form; it is the sense a boatman’s fee for work on a boat seems to need, and the lemma is only the form (ipḫi); UNCERTAIN.

sentences.i: he shall give him two shekels of silver as his gift.
sentences.n: As §228: qīštišu “as his gift”.

sentences.i: If a boatman has caulked (?) a boat for a man,
sentences.n: As §234, with the boat in the accusative (elippam, GIŠ.MÁ bare).

sentences.i: and has not made his work reliable (?), and in that very year
sentences.n: utakkilma, u-tak-ki-il-ma: the D of takālum “to trust”, “make trustworthy”; UNCERTAIN, from the stem’s meaning. ina šattimma “in the very year”: šattim with -ma, “in this same year”.

sentences.i: that boat is spoilt (?) and has acquired a fault (?),
sentences.n: elippum šī “that boat” (GIŠ.MÁ, šī “she, that”). izzapar, iz-za-par, I cannot read (it has the shape of an N-stem preterite, izzapar; a present would be izzappar; the root is not known to me); “is spoilt” is the sense the next clause needs; UNCERTAIN. ḫiṭītam, written ḫi-di-tam by Harper (DI is also ṭi): a fault; UNCERTAIN as a word. irtaši “has acquired”, as in earlier parts.

sentences.l: the-boatman that boat he-shall-tear-down-and from-the-property of-himself he-shall-make-strong-and,
sentences.i: the boatman shall tear that boat down (?) and make it strong out of his own property, and
sentences.n: inaqqarma, i-na-qar-ma (the sign GAR read qar): present of naqārum “to tear down, demolish”; UNCERTAIN. udannanma, “he shall make strong, and” (the D of danānum with -ma). ina makkūr ramānišu as in §232.

sentences.i: he shall give the owner of the boat a strong boat.
sentences.n: dannatam “strong” (feminine accusative, to match elippam “boat”, feminine): dan-na-tam. The penalty is restitution in kind, like the slave for a slave of §219.

sentences.l: If a-man his-boat to-a-boatman for-hire has-given-and,
sentences.i: If a man has given his boat to a boatman for hire,
sentences.n: elippišu “his boat”: GIŠ.MÁ with ŠU. ana malaḫim “to the boatman” (MÁ.DU.DU, bare). ana igrim “for hire”: ig-ri-im (Harper’s ig-rí-im, the sign RI); igrum “hire”. iddinma “he gave, and” (id-di-in-ma).

sentences.l: the-boatman was-careless-and the-boat has-sunk or has-destroyed,
sentences.i: and the boatman was careless and has sunk the boat or has destroyed it,
sentences.n: īgīma, i-gi-ma: preterite of egûm “to be careless, neglectful”, with -ma. uttebbi, ut-te-bi: perfect of the D of tebûm “to sink”, here transitive: “has sunk (it)”; the sense is from the stem and the law, UNCERTAIN. ù lū uḫtalliq: “or has destroyed it”. (Laws 1–10 gloss tebûm “to rise”, Š-stem “make rise”; “sink” here is the sense the law needs, with uštēliašši “raised” in §238 as its opposite.)

sentences.i: the boatman shall replace the boat for the owner of the boat.
sentences.n: iriab “he shall replace” (written i-ri-a-ab here).

sentences.l: If a-man a-boatman and a-boat he-has-hired-and,
sentences.i: If a man has hired a boatman and a boat,
sentences.n: īgurma “he hired, and”: i-gur-ma, preterite of agārum “to hire”, as in §26. malaḫam u elippam: MÁ.DU.DU and GIŠ.MÁ, both accusative and bare.

sentences.l: grain wool oil dates and anything its-name which-(is)-of ṣīnum he-has-iṣēn-her,
sentences.i: and has loaded (?) her with grain, wool, oil and dates, and whatever else there is of cargo (?),
sentences.n: Four Sumerograms in a row, each a bare word: ŠE (šeʾam “grain”), SÍG (šipâtam “wool”), Ì.GIŠ (the signs NI and GIŠ, šamnam “oil”) and ZÚ.LUM (KA and LUM, suluppam “dates”); the plate’s SÍG is the box-and-wedge sign matched to SÍG by Harper’s entry, UNCERTAIN as a shape. mimma šumšu “anything its name” is “anything whatever”. ša ṣīnim: ṣi-nim; UNCERTAIN. iṣēnši, i-ṣi-en-ši: a verb I cannot read, with -ši “her” (the boat): “has loaded her” is the context’s sense; UNCERTAIN.

sentences.l: that boatman was-careless-and the-boat has-sunk and
sentences.i: and that boatman was careless and has sunk the boat, and
sentences.n: As §236: īgīma, uttebbi (here spelled ut-te-ib-bi).

sentences.i: and has destroyed what was in her,
sentences.n: ša libbiša “what is in her”: libbiša, “her heart, interior” with -ša, the boat. uḫtalliq as in §232.

sentences.l: the-boatman the-boat which he-sank and anything which in her he-destroyed he-shall-replace.
sentences.i: the boatman shall replace the boat that he sank and whatever he destroyed in her.
sentences.n: ša utebbû “which he sank”: u-te-ib-bu-u, the same verb with the subjunctive -u. ša ina libbiša uḫalliqu “which he destroyed inside her”. iriab “he shall replace” (the penalty).

sentences.l: If a-boatman the-boat of-a-man has-sunk-and has-raised-her,
sentences.i: If a boatman has sunk a man’s boat and has raised it,
sentences.n: utebbima, u-te-ib-bi-ma: preterite of the D of tebûm “to sink”, with -ma. uštēliašši, uš-te-li-a-aš-ši: the Š of elûm “to go up”, “raise”, with -ši “her”: “has made her go up”.

sentences.i: he shall give silver, half her price.
sentences.n: kaspi “silver”: KÙ.BABBAR bare, Harper’s kaspi; mišil šīmiša “half of her price”: ŠÁM and ŠA (the plate shows two signs after the numeral; Harper prints šî-mi-ša). inaddin is restored by Harper (the last sign, IN, is drawn in outline on the plate).

sentences.i: If a man has hired a boatman,
sentences.n: A damaged stretch: the signs in square brackets are Harper’s restorations (lum; i-gur), drawn in outline or missing on the plate. Both are the forms of §237.

sentences.i: he shall give him six kor of grain a year.
sentences.n: šeššet “six”: the six wedges (three over three); ŠE.GUR “kor of grain” (ŠE and GUR, both restored by Harper); ina šanat “in the year”; inaddiššum “he shall give him”, with di and šum restored. A boatman’s hire is six kor a year.

sentences.i: If a boat of the maḫirtu (?) has struck a boat of the mukkelbītu (?)
sentences.n: The last law of the part, partly restored by Harper (square brackets: elippum, tim, uk, tim). I cannot read two of the words: maḫirtum (ma-ḫi-ir-tim) and mukkelbītum (mu-uk-ki-el-bi-tim) are two kinds of boat; the sense is unknown; UNCERTAIN. The verb comes in the next unit.

sentences.i: and has sunk it,
sentences.n: imḫaṣma “he struck, and” (as in §195ff.); uttebbi “he sank (it)”.

sentences.l: the-owner of-the-boat whose his-boat has-sunk, whatever in his-boat is-lost, before the-god he-shall-prove-and,
sentences.i: the owner of the boat whose boat has sunk shall prove, before the god, whatever was lost in his boat, and
sentences.n: The owner of the sunk boat must prove his losses by oath: ina maḫar ilim ubârma “before the god he shall prove, and”, as in §126 (ubâršuma). tebiat, te-bi-a-at, is the stative (“is sunk”) of tebûm; ḫalqu “is lost” (ḫal-qu₂, the stative with the subjunctive -u; mimma is singular); GIŠ.MÁ-šu is said elippušu (Harper’s elippu-šu, the boat as subject) and elippišu (Harper’s elippi-šu, after ina); the case vowel is the grammar’s, not written. The first ša of line 72 is the relative “whose”.

sentences.l: of-the-maḫirtu who the-boat of-the-mukkelbītu he-sank, his-boat and his-goods that-are-lost he-shall-replace-for-him.
sentences.i: the (owner) of the maḫirtu-boat who sank the boat of the mukkelbītu shall replace for him his boat and his lost goods.
sentences.n: ša maḫirtim ša … utebbû “the one of the maḫirtu who sank …”: utebbû with the subjunctive -u. iriabšum, i-ri-a-ab-šum: iriab “he shall replace” with -šum “for him” (the owner of the sunk boat). mimmâšu “his goods”, ḫalqam “lost” (Harper prints ḫal-ga-am with g; the sign is GA, read qa₂ as in earlier parts). The last law of the part, and the last of the boatmen.
